title: In a dry land (Psalm 63)
hookLine: my soul thirsts for you in a dry and weary land

cards: East of Jerusalem the land falls away fast. The green gives out, and the hills turn the color of bread crust, folding down toward the Dead Sea. Shade is a rock's width.
Water is a rumor. This is the wilderness of Judah. The heading of Psalm sixty-three puts David here, on the run.

Which time is a fair question: he fled into that wilderness from King Saul, and years later from his own son. Either way, a man with a crown, or a claim to one, is out in the dust, and his throat is dry.

teach.b: In the King James Bible the psalm begins: "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is."
The Hebrew word for soul is nephesh. It means life, self, a living being. But it can also mean the throat, the neck, the place where breath and water go in.
So when David says my soul thirsteth, a Hebrew listener could also hear: my throat is parched. The body and the longing are one word. Read that way, thirst here isn't only a pretty metaphor.
A man with a dry throat notices that what he wants most is God. Then the psalm does something unexpected for a man in a desert. It praises.
"Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee." Better than life. Better than water, then, in a place where water is life.
And it moves from dawn to night. "Early will I seek thee," it says at the start, and later, "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches."
He lies awake in the dark, in a dry land, and remembers.

teach.h: A DESERT PSALM FOR EARLY MORNING
teach.b: Because of that word early, churches pray this psalm at the start of the day.
In the Orthodox morning service it is read in the half-dark, and in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours it opens Sunday morning prayer. A desert psalm, prayed over coffee.

how: Psalm 63 is a traditional morning psalm: Orthodox Christians read it among the six psalms at the start of Matins, and Catholics pray it at Sunday Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

games.q: you're a king hiding in the desert, out of water, enemies behind you. what does the psalm do?
o: praise: thy lovingkindness is better than life.
games.why: "because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee." in a place where water is life, he names something better.

practice: If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it a moment: the weight, the cold, the light in it. Take one small sip and feel it all the way down your throat, the place the Hebrew calls nephesh, then another, without hurrying.
If you pray, let each sip carry the psalm's first words, O God, thou art my God; if you don't, just be thirsty, and drink.

wordCard.voice: Nephesh. Hebrew for soul, life, and also the throat: the word that lets my soul thirsteth also be heard as my throat is dry.

orig.note: Hebrew: soul, life, self, and also the throat. "my soul thirsteth" can be heard as "my throat is dry".

carryVoice: Your line: thirsty for God. Body and longing, one word. Four hundred twenty-six days, and counting.
